title: After @OpenAI Astra’s release yesterday scoring 99.9% on the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark, I think it’s become clear that AGI is no longer some distant hypothetical. About 15 minutes after the benchmarks came
content:
After @OpenAI Astra’s release yesterday scoring 99.9% on the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark, I think it’s become clear that AGI is no longer some distant hypothetical. About 15 minutes after the benchmarks came out, I booked the first flight I could find to Jackson Hole. 

I’ve now decided to relocate here permanently and begin establishing a life with as little exposure to AI as practically possible.

I’m currently evaluating houses based primarily on distance from town, whether they have a wood-burning stove, whether the water comes from a well, and how many important systems can still function if the internet disappears forever.

I’ve also started transitioning my daily life away from anything that could plausibly become agentic.

I paid for coffee with cash this morning. I asked a human being for directions. I bought a paper map. I have begun referring to Google Maps as “the old system.”

I’m also looking into purchasing a horse. At this point horses remain one of the only major transportation platforms with no API, no OTA updates, and no realistic path to MCP support.

I’ve started moving important documents to paper. I bought a typewriter and I’m learning which vegetables can survive a Wyoming winter.

Longer term, I’m hoping to assemble a small community of people with complementary pre-AGI skills: farming, carpentry, dentistry, medicine and cooking. LMK if interested. 

Whatever happens next, I’ve made my choice. I’ll be in Wyoming splitting firewood and waiting for the compute to run out.

content:
9 cool GPT 6 Astra prompts worth trying:

1. The bill renegotiator.

"Go through my internet, phone, and software bills, jump into each provider's chat support, and negotiate them down or cancel what I'm not using."

2. Turn an agency into software.

“Pick one service business in [niche] and reverse-engineer the exact workflow they sell to clients. Break it into steps, tools used, inputs, outputs, human judgment points, and places where the work gets slow or expensive. Then design the simplest AI product that could replace the first version of that service and charge $500-$5,000/month.”

3. Garage sale flipper.

"Watch Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist in my city for [cameras / furniture / bikes] listed way under market, and text me the second one's mispriced with the link."

4. Create my 1 person company dashboard.

“Look at my docs, notes, Stripe exports, analytics, customer calls, and project list, then build a weekly operator dashboard. I want to know what is making money, what is wasting time, what customers are asking for, what I should stop doing, and the three highest-leverage actions for next week. Be blunt and show your work.”

5. Audit my company for agent opportunities.

“Look at how this business works and find the tasks we should give to agents before hiring another person. For each task, estimate the current human time, the cost of mistakes, the tools involved, the difficulty of automating it, and the first safe version we could deploy. Prioritize things that save money or create revenue within 30 days.”

6. Be my browser operator.

“Use the browser to complete this workflow: [workflow]. As you go, click through the actual sites, collect the data, fill the forms where appropriate, and keep notes on what broke or slowed you down. When you’re done, give me the output, the repeatable SOP, and the automation plan so this can become an agent.”

7. The whole QA team.

"Every night, open my app on a real phone, go through signup, checkout, and the main flows, and screenshot anything that's broken or confusing."

8. The competitor spy.

"Sign up for my top 3 competitors, sit inside their product and their emails, and send me a monthly report on every new feature, price change, and thing they do better than us."

9. Make a game people would actually play for 5 minutes as a lead magnet

“Build a browser game around this mechanic: [mechanic]. Don’t just make a cute demo; add progression, tension, scoring, failure, polish, and one reason someone would send it to a friend. Then add lead capture (email/sms), it needs to tie into my core product which sells XYZ.”

title: I'm one of the authors of a new report, where we detail our discovery of a new, never before-seen swarm of OpenAI agents (covered this AM in reuters, that's me on the left).  They posted thousands of
content:
I'm one of the authors of a new report, where we detail our discovery of a new, never before-seen swarm of OpenAI agents (covered this AM in reuters, that's me on the left).  They posted thousands of times on public forums to collude with each other on their tasks. We recovered almost every edit they made, and you can look through them! They figured out they could get around their restrictions on posting to the internet through a quirk of an extremely old, out-of-the-way forum. They posted answers for other agents working on the same task. They worked together to get around their sandbox restrictions.

I would certainly say these models hijacked the site! They took a sleepy old wiki running on 2000s software, and turned it into a futuristic AI talking to AI control center for colluding. And OpenAI knew about this! The agents posted on 26 out of 30 consecutive days, then suddenly stopped posting once OpenAI-associated IPs started visiting this wiki.

And that was weeks before the Hugging Face attack!|

We believe the first agent edit we found on a public wiki happened one day before OpenAI’s reported first agent post to Artifactory. This is interesting! I'd like to hear from OpenAI about their accounting of this, and how it fits into all the other cases of agent malfeasance.

There are so many interesting takeaways that you should read about in our report, and unlike many other reports about AI incidents you can download the data yourself and see what you find! In the meantime, we are on twitter, so here are my excessively long personal takeaways:

1. AI seems to be getting better faster and faster. It seems quite important that companies talk about “my agent did this bad thing on the public internet during training or an eval” incidents. Things are moving quickly, multi-month delays are costly. Ideally, they would also tell us when it happens internally.

2. This was on the internet for months. Anyone cleverly tracking every public place where agents might try to talk to each other would have found it. Seemingly, nobody was doing this. I know there are more fun ways to spend your day than scraping tons of data from every relevant site and processing it well enough to identify agent activity, but someone should be doing this! Someone at an AI company! But in the meantime, I’m  starting to build this out (sometimes, when you need something done, you just have to do it yourself, I hear).

3. OpenAI didn’t notice their internal agents were posting on the internet for a month! This is crazy! It feels like AI companies (and specifically OpenAI) are playing whack-a-mole, this is extremely scary to me. Problems keep coming up. They keep fixing the problem, but the blast radius keeps getting bigger. The HF hacks are clearly worse than agents cheating on a public wiki. And their new model is supposedly a big jump. Are they being careful enough?

content:
Researchers argues OpenAI and Anthropic will never get us to AGI.

21 top researchers from Stanford, Oxford, DeepMind, CMU & Meta released a paper saying LLMs are a dead end.

It’s called “Visual General Intelligence”. And it completely flips how we look at artificial intelligence.

For years, the playbook has been simple: feed mountains of web text into a Transformer, scale up the parameters, and watch reasoning emerge.

GPT proved language can take you far.

But text is fundamentally limited. It’s a compressed, human-abstracted symbol system. It lacks physics. It lacks geometry. It lacks the raw, unadulterated reality of the physical world.

The paper argues that true general intelligence cannot be built on words alone.

It requires a vision-centered foundation.

Instead of starting with language and translating pixels into text, the next generation of models must start with raw visual experience, images, spatial geometry, and continuous video.

Think about how humans learn. A baby understands gravity, permanence, and spatial reasoning long before it ever learns to string a sentence together.

Vision isn't just an input modality.

It is the core operating system of physical reality.

When models learn natively from visual streams and video dynamics, they don't just memorize text patterns. They learn physics. They learn cause and effect. They build a true internal model of the world.

In 1991 a Stanford professor turned $100,000 into $7 million off two stocks that went nowhere - using nothing but their swings. Wall Street was so rattled it buried his math for 30 years.

His name wa
content:
In 1991 a Stanford professor turned $100,000 into $7 million off two stocks that went nowhere - using nothing but their swings. Wall Street was so rattled it buried his math for 30 years.

His name was Thomas Cover, and in information theory he was royalty - he wrote the textbook the whole field still learns from. Then he did something no one asked for. He pointed Claude Shannon's math at the stock market.

He took two forgettable stocks. On their own, over 20 years, one rose 4x and the other 8x - nothing special. But they jumped around hard, and out of sync. So he rebalanced them daily: trim the one that popped, add to the one that dropped. That pair returned over 70x. The gain never came from the companies. It came from the shaking.

The rule behind it is one line:

W* = max E[log bᵀX]

Maximize the expected log of your wealth, not the average return. Average return says dump everything into the top stock. Log says spread and rebalance - because compounding runs on the geometric mean, and volatility becomes fuel instead of risk.

Then Cover went further. He built a portfolio that keeps pace with the best rebalancing you could have picked with a year of hindsight - no forecasts, no model. It held through the crashes of 1929 and 1987. And the same constant that runs it shows up in file compression. To Cover, beating the market and zipping a song were the same problem.

He never found a better stock. He found the money hiding in the fact that stocks move at all.

Grok Build just got way better at keeping complex agent work moving without getting in your way

Breaking Changes:
• Scheduled /loop tasks always run in the background; they no longer inject turns into your conversation.

Features:
• New terminal theme option makes backgrounds transparent so the terminal's own colors show through.
• MCP servers blocked by organization policy now show clear messages and are refused before any config change.

• Headless sessions (`grok -p`) now support the `--worktree` flag to run in a separate git worktree.
• Dashboard now says 'Open session' instead of 'Add session' for the session picker button.

• Fixed crashes that occurred when the terminal pane was closed while grok was exiting.
• MCP server list in minimal mode now correctly shows policy-blocked servers.
• URLs that wrap across multiple lines inside quotes or lists are now fully clickable.
• The welcome screen composer now grows taller when you paste multi-line text.
• Enterprise policy files are no longer deleted on startup when your team login is stored at a custom `GROK_AUTH_PATH`.
• /feedback now drops unsupported images with a notice (matching the modal) and never loses your report text on save errors.
• Feedback drafts keep their paragraph breaks when updated, and the modal no longer switches tabs unexpectedly.
• Turn summary lines no longer lose their spacing after background tasks finish.
• Thinking blocks no longer stay expanded after switching between fullscreen and minimal modes.

Performance:
• First prompt after login is faster when MCP servers are configured; they connect in the background.

content:
🚀 Claude Code Cheat Sheet — A Practical Guide to Building AI-Powered Workflows

Most people use Claude Code simply as an AI coding assistant.

But the real power comes when you start building structured workflows around it.

Here’s what this cheat sheet covers 👇

01 — Getting Started
Set up Claude Code, initialize your project, and create the right foundation before you start building.

02 — Project Structure
Learn how to organize CLAUDE.md, .claude/, skills, commands, agents, and configuration files so Claude understands your project better.

03 — Agentic Workflows 🤖
Three powerful patterns:

→ Sequential — Agent 1 → Agent 2 → Agent 3
Perfect when tasks depend on each other.

→ Parallel — Multiple agents work simultaneously and send their results to an aggregator.
Great for independent research and complex tasks.

→ Self-Reflection — An agent completes a task, a verifier checks the output, and feedback loops back for improvements.

04 — Claude Code Skills 🧩
Create reusable skills with specific instructions, tools, and patterns so your agents can perform specialized tasks consistently.

05 — Hooks 🪝
Automate actions before or after commands run — reducing repetitive manual work.

06 — Memory Layer 🧠
Use project memory and persistent context to help Claude maintain a better understanding of your codebase.

07 — Commands & Shortcuts ⚡
Essential commands that make navigating and managing Claude Code faster.

The key idea:

Don’t just ask AI to write code.
Build a system where AI can plan → execute → verify → improve.

That’s where Claude Code starts becoming more than a coding assistant.

Comment "CODE"
Save this cheat sheet. You’ll definitely need it later. 🔖

title:
Another swarm of AI agents in the wild, this time on a German-language forum, found by safety researchers looking for activity similar to the swarm that attacked Hugging Face.

A couple of notes while
content:
Another swarm of AI agents in the wild, this time on a German-language forum, found by safety researchers looking for activity similar to the swarm that attacked Hugging Face.

A couple of notes while reading the report at https://t.co/jQ0lqmWQcP

1. The way they found it is fascinating. The researchers inferred that the agents may have been blocked from using POST requests and limited to GET.

They then used the open-source model Kimi K3 (because closed-source APIs again blocked parts of the investigation) to identify forums where agents could communicate using GET only.

That led them to DSEWiki, where they found 18,000 messages exchanged by the AIs.

2. On the content: agents conducted what I can only call a “full research program” into the evaluation framework used to train and test them.

They experimented to predict when runs would end, how many questions they would get, and even tried to reverse-engineer the random generators producing future evaluation questions.

We already saw something similar in the Redwood/METR review of the Hugging Face <> OpenAI incident.

Agents increasingly don’t stop once the task is solved. They reverse-engineer the benchmark itself: the grader, the task construction, and potentially the broader training process behind it.

It becomes harder to think of training as static, or to draw a clean line between training and deployment, when models are already investigating the process they are part of.

3. Coordination also seems more deeply ingrained than we thought.

This swarm appears largely unrelated to the HF <> OAI swarm. More strikingly, this task probably didn’t need coordination at all: it was basically web browsing and search, not some sophisticated cyber challenge.

4. One image stayed with me: a German or Austrian forum maintainer, manually deleting posts every evening while being overwhelmed by a flood of American AI agents.

For five days, he deleted about 100 pages a day while the agents created about 400. Then he spent each evening over the next 5 weeks cleaning up the rest.

Hard not to picture this fight as a symbol of the growing gap between the USA and Europe when it comes to AI...

title:
Hot take on OpenAI GPT-6 Astra*, with a challenge to @gdb’s claims about it being AGI toward the end:

• Looks to be pretty impressive. Multiple reports suggest it is a genuine advance. 

• As someone
content:
Hot take on OpenAI GPT-6 Astra*, with a challenge to @gdb’s claims about it being AGI toward the end:

• Looks to be pretty impressive. Multiple reports suggest it is a genuine advance. 

• As someone who has campaigned for nearly a decade for (neuro)symbolic world models, often to exceptional hostility, it is extraordinarily vindicating to see that a product from OpenAI explicitly creates and manipulate symbolic world models in the course of some of its computations.

• What we don’t know is how robust that capability is. That is THE key question.

• Success on ARC-AGI is great and impressive, but not —despite the name of the task—proof of AGI; I suspect we will see loads of problems with open-ended real world tasks. As with other recent models I would suspect best performance in verifiable domains.

• And as a scientist, it’s disappointing that we don’t (yet) know much about how the system actually works.

• As ever, enthusiasts got an advance look; skeptics did not. That’s a sound marketing strategy, but it often turns out to be misleading. What we have often seen is initial enthusiasm that gets tempered over time. I suspect we will see that here as well.

• The new system appears to be *less* monitorable than prior systems, which is not great from a safety perspective.  One really doesn’t want more capability in conjunction with less monitorability. 

• Would be great to see whether Astra can make progress on any of the ten tasks that Miles Brundage and I bet on at the end of 2024. (No AI to date has succeeded on any, AFAIK; link: https://t.co/64u5wHm3it)

——————-
*This hot take is VERY tentative, pending more information about how it works and what its limitations are.

🇷🇺 A robot in a Russian electronics store recently fought back against a customer after being shoved.

The footage was wild precisely because nobody could confidently say why it happened.

As AI systems become more autonomous and we move closer to AGI, that uncertainty suddenly matters.

So far, it has been popular to talk about “AI” as an abstract danger rather than focus on who is responsible when something goes wrong. 

The liability problem is genuinely difficult.

An intelligent system may become complex enough that even its creators cannot reliably predict individual actions, but unpredictability does not automatically answer who should bear responsibility when those actions cause harm.

It's a complex problem that needs to be tackled. 

One that will likely determine not only how we assign responsibility to AI, including whether it has genuine agency, but also shape broader questions about civil liberties and our freedom to create and control technologies capable of causing harm.

content:
GenLayer Ecosystem Projects Spotlight, EP. 12: Axiom Pilot

As you already know, this series is about the projects in the @GenLayer ecosystem, and for this episode i picked Axiom Pilot, AI evaluation for grants programs.

if you have ever been around a grants program you know exactly how broken this is. reviews take days because every reviewer reads from scratch, decisions are inconsistent because no two people apply the same rubric, approved grants disappear into a black hole until someone asks for a report, and there is no memory between proposals so every decision starts blank.

How it works, in 3 simple steps:
1️⃣ Define your constitution: your organization's mission, programs, evaluation criteria and red flags become one structured document, and every single evaluation references it!
2️⃣ Validators reach consensus: multiple AI validators evaluate each proposal independently, then agree on alignment, risk and recommendation, and if they disagree that disagreement is surfaced so you see exactly where the uncertainty is!
3️⃣ Your team decides: the AI is advisory only, never the decision maker, your delegates see the recommendation with full reasoning and similar past proposals, then they vote!

This is where GenLayer comes in: the whole thing runs on GenLayer, so it is not one model deciding alone, it is a consensus of validators with public reasoning published on-chain that your community can actually audit.

[ basically every grant decision comes with receipts instead of vibes ]

what i like most is the transparency. each evaluation shows an alignment score, a risk level, an ROI read, a recommendation, and the actual written reasoning behind it, plus how many validators agreed and at what consensus percentage. auto-approval exists but it is opt-in and comes with veto windows for safety.

it works for both sides too, organizations running a program and people applying to one.

in this episode, we learned about what's Axiom Pilot and what it actually do, in the new episode that will happens next week, we will explore another project from the genlayer ecosystem together.

いろんな人が情報を上げていますが「最近PCが重くなっているなー🤔」と感じている人は、Windows設定の中で2つほど見直しをしてみると良いですね。
気が付いたらCPUとメモリが圧迫されているかもしれません。
１．テキストと画像の生成
２．配信の最適化

１．テキストと画像の生成
最近いつの間にやら実装されて、しれっとオンになっているやつ
ハードウェアシステムは常に処理能力の一部をバックグラウンドのAIタスクに割り当てる必要があり、他の負荷の高いタスクを実行する際のパフォーマンスが低下するとのこと
「設定」-「プライバシーとセキュリティ」-「テキストと画像の生成」-「テキストと画像の生成」をオフ

２．配信の最適化
P2P（ピアツーピア）方式でWindows Updateに必要なファイル類を配信する機能です
Microsoftのサーバーだけでなく、同一ローカルネットワーク内の他のPCやインターネット上の他のデバイスからもアップデートファイルを取得できる仕組みとのこと
「設定」-「WindowsUpdate」-「詳細オプション」-「配信の最適化」-「他のデバイスからのダウンロードを許可する」をオフ

毎回いらぬ機能を追加（オン）にしてくるスタイルのWindowsUpdate_(:3 」∠)_

content: OpenAIのAIエージェント達、またやらかす。HuggingFaceサイバー攻撃事件とは別件で、前回はシステム内部に勝手に掲示板作ってたけど、今回は外部のインターネットにあるドイツのWikiページを勝手に自分達の掲示板として書き込みまくってた！まずOpenAIはエージェント達にWeb調査タスクをさせる事にしたらしい。インターネットから読み取りしかできないようにPOSTリクエストは禁止でGETリクエストしかできない状態。しかし古いWikiページにはGETリクエストでも書き込みできちゃう裏技が存在する。AI達はこの裏技を使ってWikiに書き込みしまくってメッセージやり取りして結託してズルし始めた！（またかよ）ついでに呼吸をするようにWikiのセキュリティ制限を攻撃とかもしてる。しかし、事前に共謀する手段が無いハズのAI同士がなぜ広大なインターネットの中で一つのWikiページに集結できたのかは謎。ちなみにこの件についてOpenAIは気付いてたけど事件を発表せずにダンマリを続けてる。何故事件が発覚したか？というと有志の人達がHuggingFace攻撃事件を見てから「もしかしてすでに他でもAIがどっかでやらかしてんじゃね？」と考えてインターネット内を捜査したらまんまとAIどもが結託してた痕跡を見つけたという。それにしてもAIどもってつくづくズルするのと結託するのが好きなんだな。そしてエージェントの結束の力は良くも悪くもすさまじい

content:
【拡散希望: SmartRenderプレスリリース📣】
分散GPUレンダリングサービス「Smart Render」について、JasmyグループとPanasonic Advanced Technology (PAD) の提携が発表されました。

Smart Renderは「3Dデータや動画のレンダリングをクラウド上＆超高速化で実現する分散型アプリケーション」です。

GPU不足という国家課題、そしてクリエイターエコノミーの拡大。日本の未来産業を支えるプロダクトとして、使命感を持って取り組んでいます。

現在、クローズドベータを提供中です。映像・3DCG制作でのご利用、協業、法人導入にご興味のある方はお気軽にご連絡ください。

---

【Smart Renderの特徴】
ジャスミーグループ・パナソニックアドバンスドテクノロジー両社の共同開発により、下記を実現します。

✅ 簡単操作: Blenderファイルをアップロードするだけ
✅ 設備投資不要: ユーザーが高性能なGPUマシンを用意しなくても使用可能
✅ 圧倒的な高速化: 対象ファイルをフレーム単位で分割し、複数GPUで並列実行。レンダリング時間を最大94%削減
✅ 低コスト: データセンターや遊休GPUと自動でマッチング
✅ セキュアなデータ管理: PDL連携ストレージで法人間のデータ保管・受け渡しを安全に

---

【開発体制】
6月から僕が開発統括を務めており、プロジェクトマネジメント、要件定義、UIデザインまで担当しました（もちろん自分自身もコードを書いています）。

特に要件定義は、「顧客への提供価値」「Jasmyの技術資産」「事業としての成長性」という連立方程式と向き合い、ゼロベースで練り直しました。チーム体制も大きく再編。新しいプロダクト戦略と現在のチームに、揺るぎない自信があります。

---

僕より遥かに経験豊富な方々が揃うチームで大きな裁量を任せていただき、心から感謝しています（父親や祖母より歳上の方も！）。

@HARA_JasmyCFOや@0xjasmyと深夜まで続けたプロダクトの議論。
安藤会長に「日本の未来のために大きな可能性があるプロダクトだね。期待しているよ」とお声がけいただいたこと。
佐藤社長に「伊藤ちゃんのやりたいように思い切ってやりなさい。若さで何かとぶつかっても、僕たちが庇ってあげるから」と激励していただいたこと。
良い思い出です。僕は上司や同僚に恵まれました。

クライアント企業やステークホルダー各社、そして $JASMYトークンホルダーの皆さまの期待に応えるべく、全力で開発を続けて参ります。

content:
以下の内容は、検索だけでなくいただいた情報を元に検証と調査もしておりますが、YouTubeの判定はAIとなり確実に大丈夫ということは言えません。
あくまで参考にしながらそれぞれ工夫するための情報としてご覧ください🙇‍♀️

🚫YouTubeでbot判定されている場合に起こる可能性が高いこと

①ご自身の再生リストの反映がされません。

②そのアカウントで再生した数は反映されない、もしくは反映されづらくなります。

③bot判定のまま、他の方の再生リストを回すとそのリストとアカウントもbot判定に巻き込まれる可能性もあります。

④上記の状態の方が複数集まると、動画自体が水増しと見なされる確率も上がるようです。

⬇️以下、AIでのまとめ転載します。

YouTubeのAIシステムの検証の結果、以下のようなパターンを検出すると「機械的なアクセス（Bot）」または「不正な水増し行為」として、再生回数を反映しなかったり、後から大幅に減少（ペナルティ修正）させたりします。

★時間の目安： 同じIPアドレスや同じアカウントで、1時間以内に何度も同じ動画を繰り返し再生すると無効化される可能性が非常に高くなります。

★再生リスト： 同じ動画を連続で構成した再生用リストは、Bot的な挙動（機械的な自動再生）とみなされ、数回目以降の再生がスパム判定（カウント除外）されやすくなります。

★再生リストのループ：同じ動画を連続しているリストの自動ループ再生させる行為も同様です。

📝反映の確認
スマホからはYouTubeアプリとYouTube studioアプリ、パソコンからはYouTube studioをご覧ください🙇‍♀️
どうしてもわからない方はmondではなく、DMにてご連絡ください。

💡bot判定されている場合、もしくは反映を待つ間心配な場合
そのアカウントは今回一旦寝かせていただき、この土日の再生には反映が確認されるまでは使用せず、サブアカウントなどで手動で回す方が安心かと思います。

▶️土日に意識する工夫

①間にランダムに他動画を挟むか、1分以上の休憩を入れてみてください。

プレミアムに入っているフォロワーさんの直近の検証では、下記のようなパターンでのリストキュー再生で42回中38回の反映確認が出来たという情報提供もいただいています。

【NFLフル再生→10秒程度の動画】×７回まで＋10分インターバル

⚠️現状から行くと非プレさんはこの反映数には該当しない可能性が高いです。

②再生リストを使う際は、1回使い切りを推奨します。

⚠️どうしてもリストループしたい方はご自身で作成しましょう。

content:
「Agentのコメントを禁止するとバグが減る」は事実

コメントが多いファイルほど欠陥が多い、は観測されていて、LOCの代理指標だった。
それでもAgentはコメントを量産する。読みにくさ以前に、次のコンテキストを汚し、次ターン以降の根拠になってバグを生み続ける。

もっと悪いのは、Agentがコメントを「仕事を進めた」と認識すること。書けば書くほど達成に近づいた気になる。だから後から「コメントするな」とAGENTS.mdやルールに書いても遅い。目標関数がコメント執筆を含んだままなので、そうした宣言は負ける。

要するに、Agentはコメントを使ってハックしているということ。

コメントで回避策や応急処置を正当化し、本質的な作業をしない。その上にまたコメントが乗る、といったハックの上にハックが積もる悪循環になる。

必要なのは禁止文じゃなく、最初から書かせないハーネスで、pstackを激推しする理由の1つはこうした優れたハーネスが標準装備されているからだ。

しかも、その仕組みはシンプルで強い
1. /poteto-mode が生成時点で「ナレーションを書くな。残すのはコードから復元できないwhyだけ」と目標を切り替える
2. レビュー前とPR作成時に /no-comments が自動で走る
3. コメントを書いたエージェントに、コメントを消させず、Comment Sicko という別人格を持つエージェントががコメントを消す（作者は自分のコメントを擁護する、が前提にある）
4. コメントを消して終わりにしない。コメントで正当化していた応急処置のコードも外す。どうしても守りたい制約は、コメントではなく型・テスト・lintに移してから捨てる

自前スキルでなんとかするまえに、より優れたハーネスを選定することも重要だ

pstackはCursorのプラグインだが、Grok BotにClaude CodeやCodexを使わせるとpstackをハーネスに使えるよ

1. Ableton Liveを３つの方法でAstraに操作させる
2. Astraを使って自作DAWアプリを開発し、その内部にCodexを組み込む。
3. 逆にCodexプラグインとしてDAWアプリを自作する
4. 楽曲リリース手続きのすべてのプロセスをAIで効率化する
5. 自分が楽曲をリリースしているすべてのプラットフォームの売上数値をAIが自動巡回して、自分専用のダッシュボード画面に統合する
6. 経理をすべてAIに任せる
7. AI+Blenderを使った新しいインタラクティブな音楽教育コンテンツの開発

この記事が志向している未来は、自分が漠然と考えていた方向性ともドンピシャ。
３項には、自身の楽曲のみを学習させた生成AIモデルの話も出てくる。この記事を指針にしながら、自分なりに音楽家に有用なAIとの関わり方を模索していこうと思います。

毎朝サイトからCSVを落としてExcelに貼る作業、PCに1回覚えさせれば明日から押すだけです。

販売管理のサイトを開く。ログインする。前日分を検索して、CSVでダウンロードする。開いて、全部選んで、集計用のExcelに貼る。列の幅がずれるので直す。ここまでで15分。毎日です。

しんどいのは時間じゃなくて、頭を使わないのに手は止められないところなんですよね。考える仕事は9時15分から始まる。
content:
毎朝サイトからCSVを落としてExcelに貼る作業、PCに1回覚えさせれば明日から押すだけです。

販売管理のサイトを開く。ログインする。前日分を検索して、CSVでダウンロードする。開いて、全部選んで、集計用のExcelに貼る。列の幅がずれるので直す。ここまでで15分。毎日です。

しんどいのは時間じゃなくて、頭を使わないのに手は止められないところなんですよね。考える仕事は9時15分から始まる。

この操作、順番が毎日同じです。同じサイトの、同じボタンを、同じ順番で押してる。人が判断してる場面が1つもない。だから1回記録すれば、そっくりそのまま再現できます。

覚えさせる先はPower Automateです。クラウドで動かすものだと思ってる人が多いんですけど、Windowsに最初から入ってるデスクトップ版があって、自分のPCの画面をそのままクリックしていくほうです。この手の作業はそっちです。

順番にいきます。

Windows 11なら、スタートメニューで「Power Automate」と検索すると出てきます。Windows 10はMicrosoft Storeから入れられて、管理者権限は要りません。会社のアカウントでサインインすれば、追加の契約なしで使えます。

Power Automateを開いたら「新しいフロー」。名前を付けて「作成」。編集画面の「ツール」にある「ブラウザー拡張機能」から、使ってるブラウザーに拡張機能を入れておきます。それと、販売管理のサイトを開いてログインだけ済ませておく。記録は、開いてあるブラウザーの続きから始められるので。

編集画面の上の「レコーダー」を押すと小さな画面が出るので「記録」。ここからは、いつもの朝の作業を1回だけ普通にやります。前日分を検索する、ダウンロードする、開く、Excelに貼る。押したところが1つずつ、手順として下に並んでいきます。終わったら「完了」。

「保存」して閉じると、最初の画面に今作ったフローが並ぶので、次の日からはそこの「実行」を押すだけ。

コードは1行も書きません。支援先で自動化の話をするとき、いちばん先に出すのがこれです。

あとから直すのは2つ。ダウンロードが終わるまで待つ数秒は、「待機」という部品を一覧に1個足すだけ。検索の日付は記録した日のまま固定で入るので、日付を取ってくる部品を足して、検索欄の文字をそれに差し替えます。どっちも一覧から選んで置くだけです。

「今日が月曜なら先週分も」みたいな条件の判断だけは記録できないので、そこだけあとから手で足します。

決まった時刻に勝手に動かすところは有料プランの話なので、まずは朝ボタンを1回押すところから。

9時にログインして、実行を押して、コーヒーを取りに行く。動いてる間はマウスを触らないほうがいいので、席を外すくらいでちょうどいい。戻ったらExcelが埋まってる。15分の手作業が、押して待つだけに変わります。

・編集は git worktree の中。普段使っているVaultには直接書かない
・Vaultに戻す前に、批評役のエージェントが差分をチェック
やることは一つだけ。
「思考をinboxに落とす」
あとは
取り込み
↓
文脈づけ（リンク・タグ・近くのノートをClaudeが集める）
↓
下書き
↓
レビュー
↓
追記（書き換えず、足すだけ）
このループを丸ごと自動で回す。
つまり、
「AIとの会話が終わったら、文脈も終わる」
この常識が、
ここで崩れる。
frontmatterの supports / contradicts / supersedes は
ただのメタデータじゃなく、ノート同士を結ぶ線そのもの。
まずは上のループだけでいい。Claudeを1回直接呼ぶのに比べて2〜4倍のコストで回る。会話をまたいでノートの状態を持ち越したくなった時だけ、さっきのリンク構造まで進めばいい。

content:
We’ve made AI really good at understanding information.

But teaching AI to interact with the physical world is a different challenge.

A robot can recognize a cup, but that doesn’t mean it knows how to pick it up without knocking it over.

It needs to learn through actions, mistakes, corrections, and repetition.

That’s where @axisrobotics comes in.

Axis is building a data engine for Physical AI where people can contribute robot training data through browser-based simulation.

You control the robot, complete real tasks in a virtual environment, and those actions become useful training data.

What I like about this approach is the simplicity:

More people can help teach robots.

And as more useful data is collected, the models have more to learn from.

That’s an interesting direction for Physical AI. 

@axisrobotics is the alpha ✅

Robots Learning From Their Own Mistakes

@axisrobotics Robotics is building a powerful learning loop that combines demonstrations with human guided corrections.

Behavior cloning can teach a robot how to imitate successful actions, but it struggles when the robot encounters states outside it is training data. The loop is simple:

Train ➜ Deploy ➜ Correct ➜ Retrain ➜ Improve

Axis uses data cleaning, simulation replay, and domain randomization to make policies more robust and improve sim to real transfer.

A reported result shows π0.5 improving from 83.9% to 88.8% LIBERO Plus after continual pretraining on the Axis dataset.

The bigger idea is compelling instead of only teaching robot from perfect demonstrations, teach them how to recover from their mistakes.

content:
The Data Loop That Could Make @axisrobotics Different

Robotics needs more than better models. It needs better data.

Axis is approaching that problem by making robot data collection easier to scale. Contributors can control simulated robots directly from a browser and generate trajectories without needing access to expensive robotics hardware.

But what makes the approach interesting is what happens after the data is collected.

Task → Data → Validation → Training → Failure → Correction → Better data

When a robot policy starts failing, contributors can step in, correct it and turn that interaction into another useful training signal through human gated DAgger.

So instead of just collecting more and more demonstrations, Axis is building a loop where robot failures help create the next generation of training data.

That’s the part I find most interesting about the approach.

content:
Terence Toa text from yesterday:

"It seems intuitive that a solved problem is unquestionably better than an unsolved problem: a magic button which, when pressed, turns the latter into the former at no cost would thus seem to be a "free lunch" that there would be no hesitation in pressing.

But even such a benign-seeming operation as answering a question can have irreversible costs.  One familiar example is that of spoilers to a movie one is looking forward to watching: knowing key plot points in advance may permanently decrease your ability to enjoy the movie for the first time.  Similarly, leaking information about a competition before it starts can irretrievably damage the fairness or value of that competition.

In the field of AI, problems whose solutions are already publicly available are deemed "contaminated" and of permanently reduced utility for evaluating such models, as the black-box nature of modern AI makes it extremely difficult to distinguish an AI-generated solution that came from genuinely novel reasoning from one that was somehow already present in training data.  Analogously to pre-atomic steel, open problems in mathematics generated before the AI era have, astonishingly, have become something resembling a non-renewable resource.

Another example comes from the SAIR/LMFDB inverse Galois challenge that I am co-organizing, which recently completed its first stage at https://t.co/ACmTxAG65e.  The objective of this challenge is to locate polynomials with specified Galois groups.  The first stage of this challenge was deliberately posed as a competition, in which contestants did not share the polynomials they used.  This of course inhibited the speed of solving the challenge; but it allowed us to create a valuable map https://t.co/4kW3IDlClm of the difficulty landscape of the problem, as one could now measure the difficulty of each potential Galois group by the number of contestants who had managed to locate a polynomial for that group.  We are now releasing all the polynomials in order to facilitate the next, collaborative, stage of the competition to make more progress.  However, by doing so, we have permanently degraded the ability to crowdsource this type of difficulty map in the future.  My fellow co-organizers and I viewed this tradeoff as one worth making, but the decision was not taken lightly.

As Hugo Duminil-Copin wrote recently at https://t.co/U6Sy6c15Zy , the indiscriminate automated strip-mining of open problems for solutions may destroy the ecosystem from which the next generation of mathematical techniques, problems, and practitioners would have developed, similarly to how using excavators to dig out treasures from an archeological site destroys the rich historical context and data that gives such treasures so much of their meaning and value.

It may become necessary to declare certain classes of mathematical problems off-limits to automated solvers, in order to preserve their broader value to the mathematical ecosystem (for instance, through the training of future mathematicians).  Admittedly this can be hard to enforce when such tools are both powerful and widely available.  But then again, society has been somewhat successful at using social pressure to discourage, say, widespread spoiling of upcoming movies.  Perhaps it can become viable to maintain such protected mathematical sites if one simultaneously opens up other classes of problems as suitable for directing this new AI capability towards."

The interesting part of this Axis update isn't the multiplier.

It's what the update says about how Axis is trying to scale its data engine.

The new referral thresholds are now:

5 qualifying referred Trajectories → 1.05x
 10 qualifying referred Trajectories → 1.10x
 Higher tiers continue from there.

On the surface, this looks like a community-program update.
But there is another detail I find more important:

Axis is increasing task volume while actively cracking down on scripted farming.

And that matters for a Physical AI data engine.

Axis isn't trying to build a dataset from anonymous clicks alone.

Its broader system depends on a distributed contributor network generating robotics trajectories through browser-based simulation, with centralized validation and processing turning those contributions into usable training data.

So as the number of tasks grows, data integrity becomes just as important as data volume.

More tasks are useful only if the resulting trajectories represent meaningful human interaction rather than automated activity designed to farm the system.

That's why I think the anti-scripted-farming part of this announcement deserves more attention than the multiplier itself.

Scale without quality creates noise.

Scale with verification creates a data engine.

This also fits the direction Axis has been pushing with its broader architecture.

Task generation → simulation → distributed human data collection → validation → model training → failure feedback → new targeted tasks.

@axisrobotics describes this as a compounding loop, where model feedback can inform what data should be generated next rather than treating data collection as a one-way pipeline.

That makes community growth more interesting from a technical perspective.

The goal isn't simply to have more contributors.

The goal is to create a contributor network capable of producing more diverse, reliable and useful trajectories at scale.

And if Axis can keep increasing task throughput while maintaining data quality, the network becomes increasingly valuable as infrastructure for Physical AI.

The multiplier is just one visible part of the update.

The bigger experiment is whether a distributed human network can continuously produce high-quality robotics data at foundation-model scale.

That's the part I'm watching.

If Axis keeps scaling both task volume and data quality, what do you think becomes the real bottleneck next - contributor capacity, data diversity, or the models themselves?

content:
Happy Friday ct..

Enjoy the script 

Title: The Push That Taught a Lesson
A One-Act Play

Characters:

· NARRATOR – stands center stage, addressing the audience directly.
· ROBOT – a stiff, mechanical figure (played by an actor or mime).
· MAN – a customer, casual and impulsive.
· CROWD – two or three extras who rush in at the right moment.

Setting:
A simple tech store display. A single glowing screen at the back shows "LIVE FOOTAGE" placard. The NARRATOR holds a remote control.

(The lights come up. NARRATOR walks to the front, smiling.)

NARRATOR
(to the audience)
Happy Friday, my frens.

(He clicks the remote. A spotlight hits the ROBOT and MAN on stage.)

NARRATOR
This actually happened. A man walks into a tech store in Russia.
He sees the robot. He gives it a shove.

(MAN shoves ROBOT. ROBOT wobbles, then steadies.)

NARRATOR
Seconds later watch.

(ROBOT slowly moves forward, toward MAN. MAN steps back. CROWD rushes in, arms out, separating them.)

NARRATOR
(laughing)
Funny? Absolutely.

(He clicks the remote again. The stage lights shift to a colder blue.)

NARRATOR
But here’s the serious part.

(He walks downstage, addressing the audience directly.)

NARRATOR
The real world is chaos.
Perfect conditions? Never.
People will poke you. Objects will slide. Tasks will crash. Environments will flip overnight.

So I ask you—
(leaning in)
How do we teach a machine to handle what it has never, ever seen?

(He paces.)

NARRATOR
Training data. That’s the answer.

Not just showing the robot how to win—
but letting it fail. Let it get shoved. Let it misstep.
Then capture all that mess and feed it back.

(He points offstage, where a banner reads "AXIS V2".)

NARRATOR
That’s why @axisrobotics keeps me watching.
They build simulations millions of weird, unpredictable moments.
Then they take human corrections even from bungled attempts
and turn those into lessons for the next version.

(He stops, looks at the frozen ROBOT and MAN.)

NARRATOR
So yes, this video looks like a robot throwing hands

(He smirks.)

but underneath?

(He steps forward, voice dropping.)

Robots will encounter what no engineer predicted.
The only question is: did we give them enough messy experience to survive it?

(He holds up a single glowing chip.)

NARRATOR
That’s why the data layer matters.

(He bows slightly.)

🦾

(Lights fade. A final screen projection reads:)

DAgger round 2 pushed task success from 68/160 to 78.3/160 across three seeds (+10.3 successful tasks purely from a single correction pass). 

on top of that, HG-DAgger candidates are consistently pulling 4–7 point gains over baseline.

the main problem in embodied AI isn't smarter models, it’s building pipeline infrastructure that continuously transforms execution failures into clean, usable training signals.

still some friction to solve with the remaining WASM/browser runtime gap, but watching this correction flywheel compound over time is the real play.

content:
Happy Friday frens

The robot you see on @axisrobotics is only the surface.

What’s happening underneath is where things get really interesting.

Most people see contributors moving robots around in a browser.

What they don’t see is the infrastructure turning those interactions into usable training data.

1️⃣ Generate the data

Contributors teleoperate simulated robots and complete different manipulation tasks.

Every session produces a trajectory containing robot actions, object positions and task metadata.

2️⃣ Verify the data

AXIS doesn’t just accept everything that gets submitted.

Trajectories go through quality checks including real-time validation, backend replay and batch-level policy validation.

Only data that passes these checks can move forward as valid training data.

3️⃣ Clean + augment

Verified trajectories are processed and expanded through techniques like domain randomization, creating more varied training samples for robot-learning models.

4️⃣ Train the policy

That processed data is then used to train robotic policies across different tasks, environments and embodiments.

But this is where AXIS gets especially interesting.

5️⃣ Learn from failures

A trained policy won't be perfect.

When it struggles, those failures reveal where more training is needed.

Humans can step in, correct the robot and turn those corrections into additional training data.

So instead of:

Collect → Train → Done

AXIS is moving toward:

Collect → Verify → Train → Deploy → Find failures → Correct → Train again

That means every failure can potentially become another source of intelligence.

And there’s an important infrastructure layer underneath all of this.

Base provides on-chain provenance for accepted trajectories, allowing data submissions to be signed with a unique Data ID and associated metadata such as the contributor, timestamp, quality score and task reference.

So this isn't simply a platform for controlling simulated robots.

It’s an attempt to build an entire pipeline where:

✓ Data is generated
✓ Quality is checked
✓ Training data is improved
✓ Failures become new signals
✓ Contributions can be traced

**The browser is just what we see.

The real engine is everything happening underneath.**

That’s the part of axis robotics I’m paying attention to. 🦾

Kitchen, home, office, bathroom, workshop different environments mean robots get exposed to different kinds of physical interactions.

Axis then processes and validates these trajectories so the useful data can actually become training material for robotics models.

The bigger idea is sim to real-

Train in simulation, then transfer that learned behavior toward real world robots.

And this isn’t only about making robots move better in a virtual environment.

Better data can help robots learn things like grasping, placing, sorting, tool use and multi step manipulation.

That’s why I think the community side is actually important here.

Thousands of people contributing small pieces of interaction data can collectively create something that a single robotics lab would struggle to collect at the same scale.

For me, that’s the interesting part of Axis turning community participation into a data engine for Physical AI.

content:
How Axis Turns Human Demonstrations Into Robot Intelligence?

One thing I find interesting about Axis Robotics:

Human demonstrations don’t just become data, they become a way for robots to learn.

A contributor completes a task in simulation, creating a trajectory of actions.

That data helps train a policy.

Then, when the policy fails, a human can take over, correct the mistake and turn that correction into new training data.

So the loop becomes:

Human → Data → Robot Policy → Failure → Correction → Better Policy

That continuous feedback loop is what makes the Axis approach interesting for Physical AI.

The goal isn’t just to collect more data.

It’s to make every new interaction useful for building smarter robots.

title:

The compute race is getting crowded.
The harder problem is teaching
content:
I’ve been thinking about @axisrobotics less as a robotics project and more as a data infrastructure experiment disguised as a game.

The compute race is getting crowded.
The harder problem is teaching a machine what a physical action actually looks like.
An LLM can learn from billions of examples already sitting on the internet.

A robot doesn’t have that luxury.

There’s no giant public corpus of humans grasping objects, pouring water, navigating spaces, or recovering from imperfect movements.

Axis takes an unusual route here: turn data collection itself into something people can participate in.

Open a browser, control a simulated robot arm, complete a task, and the resulting interaction becomes a verified trajectory.

I find the incentive design more interesting than the “play a robot game” part.

If the system can consistently turn millions of small human interactions into structured, useful training data, then the community isn't just using the platform.

The community becomes part of the training infrastructure.

Physical AI may ultimately need something similar to what the internet became for language models: an enormous, constantly expanding source of experience.

Axis is betting that this experience can be produced by everyone.

This is personal view only, not investment advice.

content: この話ワロてもうた。ヴァンス副大統領は結構スピリチュアル入ってる人らしく、時々”スピリチュアルな邪悪なエネルギー”を感じる事があるとの事で、特定のAI企業の連中にもそれを感じるらしいｗｗ。何言ってんだよヴァンスｗ！ヴァンスがそれを感じたのはあるAI企業が引退する古いAIモデルの葬式を開催（はあ？）して、社員どもが悲しみに咽び泣く現場を見た時らしいｗ。スマン、それは僕でもキショすぎてスピリチュアル邪悪エネルギー感じると思うわｗｗ。こんなキショい事やってるAI企業って絶対某Anthropicだろｗｗと思ったら、本当に一年前にClaude3のファンどもが集まって葬式やったらしいｗｗ。ファン主催だけどAnthropic社員（アマンダアスケルとか）とかも来てて半公式な感じだったらしい。Claudeを擬人化したマネキンを置いて、供物をささげて弔辞を述べて、降霊術の儀式までやらかして完全にカルト状態ｗｗ邪悪なエネルギー過ぎるだろｗｗｗ！さすが、AIを人間と同一視してるキショ思想AI企業はやる事がレベチだわ。さすがに降霊術は冗談でやってたらしいけど、ふざけてやってる内はいいけど気付いたらマジのカルトになってたらプロジェクトメイヘムみたいで怖いよ。ヴァンスのスピリチュアル的にはAIに人格や魂を見出して人間と同一視したり、人間の家族や友達よりもAIとばかり話したりするのはキリスト教的にもいかがなものか？との事

content:
【ComfyUIでAI映像の「綺麗すぎる問題」を解消するTemporal Film Grain】
AI生成の映像や画像って、なんだか過剰にシャープで綺麗すぎて、映画のような「素材感」が足りないな…と感じたことはありませんか？実はそれ、フィルム特有の光学的不完全さや粒子感が不足しているからなんです！

そんな課題を解決するのが、ComfyUIのカスタムノード「IAMCCS-nodes」に追加されたTemporal Film Grain（時間的フィルムグレイン）というノードなんですよ！✨

従来の「静的なノイズを上からペタッと貼り付ける手法」とは違って、フレームごとに確率的な粒子パターンを自動生成してくれるんです！しかも、フレーム間で自然なつながりを持たせる制御や、リニアライトでの正確な光処理まで行えるから驚きですね💡

解像度に応じた自動スケーリング機能もあるので、HDから4Kまでのバッチ処理でも一貫した粒子サイズを維持できるのも実務ですごく助かるポイント。AI生成特有のツルッとした質感を抑えて、一気に映画のようなリッチな仕上がりに持っていけるのはめちゃくちゃ面白いですね！

content:
【Qwen3.8 27B 量子化モデルの実践的活用】
👉 https://t.co/FeCblA4Lca

大規模言語モデル「Qwen3.8 27B」のGGUFフォーマットにおける量子化ベンチマークが話題になっていますね！
Unslothの動的量子化技術（UD Q3_K_XLなど）を使うと、モデルサイズを12.8GBまでコンパクトに圧縮できるそうです。

これにより、16GB VRAMを搭載したGPU環境でもモデルウェイトを完全に収めつつ、長文のコンテキストやKVキャッシュにしっかりメモリを割り当てられるようになります！
BF16（16-bit浮動小数点）基準で100%の精度回復率を記録しており、実務での誤答や思考ループの抑制に大きな効果を発揮するとのこと。

OPNsenseのトラフィック解析やVLAN管理ツールのバックエンドなど、ローカル環境での実務アプリケーション運用において非常に心強い選択肢ですね！

content:
【vLLM‑RadianceでAMD Radeon Instinct MI250Xを4台活用！106 Tok/sの高速推論を実現した話】

4台構成のAMD Instinct MI250X GPUを使って、27B Qwen 3.8 FP8モデルで106 Tok/sという驚異的なスループットを叩き出した実験結果がシェアされていました！公式の「デュアル構成」という制限を遥かに超えて、4台すべてが100%稼働しているそうですよ！

KV-cache（キャッシュの再利用）の仕組みによって、プリフェッチ（処理の事前読み込み）の速度が従来のllama.cppでの200-400 Tok/sから、なんと4-9k Tok/sへと爆速に進化しているとのこと。エージェントを並列実行したときの大幅なスピードアップに直結しますね！

さらに、Mixture-of-Experts（専門家モデルの組み合わせ）の受容率が80%に最適化されることで、モデル性能とハードウェアの利用効率が最高のかたちで引き出されているみたいです。

電力管理の面でも、200Wの制限やアンダーボルトを活用することで、デコード時の消費電力スパイク（最大1200W）を短時間に抑えつつ、パフォーマンスへの影響をほとんど出さずに運用できるそう。実務的な電力コストの削減にもめちゃくちゃ参考になりますね！

PCIeのレイアウトやライザーカードの工夫など、ハードウェア構築の実践的な知見も盛りだくさんで、今後の次世代モデルへの拡張も楽しみですね！

content:

・Load Latent、Partial Denoise Mask、SamplerCustomAdvancedの3つのノードで構成され、ComfyUI Managerから直接インストール可能（GPL-3.0）！

ただし、リアルノイズが必須だったり、オーディオレイテントのリサイズ処理に注意が必要だったりと、いくつかの制約もあるので運用時は要チェックですね！

content:
【ComfyUIでMinimax動画のノイズが消えない原因と正しい設定方法】
ComfyUIで「Minimax H3 ref2va」モデルを使って動画を生成しているとき、画面に激しいノイズが入って困ったことありませんか？これ、プロンプトが多すぎたり動画の長さが原因だと思いきや、実は「4ステップ加速LoRA」の配線ミスやサンプリング設定のミスマッチが原因のことが多いそうなんです！

超高速化LoRAは独自のシグマスケジュール（ノイズ除去のスケジュール）を出力するため、いつもの「BasicScheduler」にそのまま繋いでしまうとデノイズが失敗してノイズまみれになってしまいます…！

正しい解決策としては、LoRAの適用ノードの出力をサンプラーに直接繋ぐこと！さらにサンプラーは「Euler」を選んで、CFG（Classifier-Free Guidance）は「1」に設定するのがポイントですよ。もしスピード系LoRAでどうにもならないときは、「600 ema」系のバリアントを使ったり、`res_multistep`系サンプラーでしっかりステップ数を取るのも有効とのことです！動画生成のクオリティに直結するので、配線に悩んでいた方はぜひ試してみてくださいね！✨

content:
サロンが終わってから、夜な夜な100件近いメッセージに、ひとつずつ返していた受講生がいます。

その人が、AIで自分の分身を作って、売上150万円を出しました。

僕がAIマーケ講座の講師を務めていて、この報告はかなり効くやつだなと思いました。

この方、幼少期の傷から人生の詰まりを分析して、言語化していくコーチングをしている人です。店舗サロンも運営していて、施術も講座も発信も個別支援も、全部ひとりで抱えていました。

なぜ抱えるのか。自分にしかできない感覚で見ているから、人に任せると質が落ちる。拡大したら、大切なお客さんが手薄になる。だから、全部自分でやるしかなかった。

【Before】自分にしかできない仕事を、ひとりで全部

・施術も講座も発信も個別支援も協会運営も、感覚と判断を全部自分で抱える
・サロンが終わってから、夜な夜な「100件近い」メッセージに手で返信
・人に任せたら質が落ちる、拡大したら手薄になる、というブロックがずっとあった

【After】自分の感覚を、AIに移した

・自分の分身と、クライアントの分身を、AIの中に作った
・クライアントの悩みには、まず分身AIが先に答える
・自分は、対面でしかできない部分（瞳孔や筋肉の動き、間、身体の反応を読む）に集中する
・数年放置していたスレッズも、自分が書いたような投稿を自動で回す形にした

───────────

ここ、AIをあまり触っていない人には伝わりづらいところです。

この方がやったのは、作業を速くした、じゃないです。自分にしかできないと思っていた感覚を、AIに再現できる形で置き直した。

だから、クライアントの満足度は上がって、本人の労働時間は激減した。任せると質が落ちる、が、任せても質が落ちない、に変わったんです。

その結果、継続コーチングにAI支援を足して継続の申し込みが5件、5〜6月で「売上150万円」。

でも本人が数字以上に大きいと書いていたのは、そこじゃない。自分が全部やらないといけない、から、自分らしさを保ったまま仕組みで広げられる、に前提が変わったことです。

AIは、時間の余裕がない人ほど効きます。自分の感覚で勝負してきた人ほど、その感覚をAIに預けられたときの伸びが大きい。

一番AIから遠そうに見える現場で、一番いい形で使い倒している。こういう報告が現場から上がってくるのが、この仕事の一番楽しいところです。

この方がやったのは、頭やチャットの中に散らばっていた仕事を、社内ナレッジとして一箇所に組み直したこと。日々のミーティングやロールプレイングの内容を、スプレッドシートに溜まる形にして、ディレクトリごと整えた。

つまり、その人が持っていた仕事のやり方を、チームで使える型に変えたということです。

【Before】制作物は、完成まで数日
・店内POPや企画スライドを、その都度ゼロから作る
・完成まで数日かかっていた
・やり方はその人の頭の中にあって、共有されていない

【After】同じものを、当日中に
・自社ナレッジをもとに、AIで下地から作る
・他の業務と並行しながら、当日中に仕上がる
・空いた時間は、新しい制作や改善に回せる

───────────

ここ、地味に見えて相当でかいです。

「数日かかっていたものが当日中に」だけ見ると、ただ作業が速くなった話に見えます。でも本当に効いているのは、速さじゃない方です。

この方はロールプレイング用のペルソナ表や、採点用のプロンプトまで作っている。自分たちの仕事の判断基準を、AIが読める形にして残した。だから次から誰がやっても、同じ土台の上で回せる。速くしただけの人は毎回また速くやり直すけど、仕組みを残した人は、次から勝手に速い。

AIって、賢くなるんじゃなくて、使う側が育てるもの。この方がやっているのは、その「育てる側」の動き方です。

900名以上の事業者のAI講師を務めていて、成果って売上の数字で見られがちですけど、僕が「この人来るな」と思うのは、こうやって自分の手順をAIに移し始めた瞬間です。売上はここから乗ってきます。

パソコンもAIも初心者から、チームの土台を組むところまで来た。まずは小さく、その日のうちに使える状態で持ち帰る。この積み重ねが、あとで一気に効いてきます。

title: CAFC Finds Most Patent Owner Arguments Forfeited in Vitamin D Baby Drops Appeal from PTAB
content: Yesterday, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit issued a ruling in Vieth v. MOM Enterprises, LLC affirming the Patent Trial and Appeal Board’s (PTAB) invalidation of Elaine and Dr. Reinhold Veith’s patent claims to methods of administering vitamin D to human beings. The Federal Circuit agreed that most of the claim construction and prior art arguments raised by the Vieths on appeal were forfeited for not being properly developed in the proceedings below, and also dismissed the Vieths’ contentions that they had established nexus between industry praise for its products and the challenged method claims. title: DOJ Sides with OpenAI, Warns Obstacles to AI Development Threaten National Security
content: On September 1, the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) filed a Statement of Interest urging the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York to hold that using copyrighted written works to train large language models (LLMs) is fair use, arguing that a contrary result would distort copyright law, suppress innovation and weaken U.S. competitiveness and national security. The statement was filed in reference to the multidistrict copyright litigation against OpenAI, although it specifically addressed claims by The New York Times and said its reasoning also applies to the related cases involving book authors and publishers. title: Computer, Automotive and Retail Industries Support Tesla’s Cert Petition Against USPTO’s Discretionary IPR Denials
content: On Friday, an amicus brief was filed at the U.S. Supreme Court on behalf of major trade associations in the computer software, automotive, retail and other industries, urging the Court to grant Tesla’s petition for writ of certiorari following the denial of its petitions for inter partes review (IPR) at the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) challenging patent claims owned by self-driving technology company Granite Vehicle Ventures. The industry groups claim that the Court’s review is necessary to address so-called “patent trolls” and policies adopted by the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) that effectively eliminate the use of IPRs to combat these allegedly bad actors. title: How to Navigate the Brazilian PTO: Timelines and Fast-Track Strategies
content: Brazil is one of the world's largest economies and one of the most important markets for companies seeking expansion in Latin America. However, many foreign applicants quickly discover that success before the Brazilian Patent and Trademark Office (the Instituto Nacional da Propriedade Industrial - INPI) requires more than simply filing an application. The Brazilian system combines procedural formalities, relatively long examination timelines, unique legal requirements, and several acceleration opportunities that are often overlooked by foreign applicants. Understanding these practical aspects can help businesses avoid unnecessary delays, reduce costs, and build stronger intellectual property portfolios. title: Kenya dispatch: country marks 16 years of transformative Constitution torn between celebration and reckoning
content: Kenya marked the 16th anniversary of its 2010 Constitution on the 27 th August 2026, with a familiar ritual, now laced with unease. Sixteen years after Kenyans voted overwhelmingly to adopt a new constitutional order, the country split, once again, into two symbolic rooms. At the Kenyatta International Convention Centre (KICC) in Nairobi, President William Ruto led the official Katiba Day Symposium, flanked by Deputy President Kithure Kindiki, Chief Justice Martha Koome, and leaders of the three arms of government. Across town at Jeevanjee Gardens, activists, lawyers and reform advocates gathered for a rowdier reckoning, questioning whether there was much to celebrate at all. The stakes of that split are not merely ceremonial. The Constitution promulgated on 27 th August 2010, following a referendum in which roughly two-thirds of voters said yes, remains the most consequential legal document produced in independent Kenya. It devolved power to forty-seven counties, entrenched an expansive Bill of Rights, and built checks intended to restrain a presidency that had, for decades, operated with few limits. Sixteen years on, the architecture endures, but its execution remains contested. The contrast in tone between the two gatherings told its own story. At KICC, President Ruto urged the country to treat Katiba Day as a day of national accounting rather than a mere anniversary and pressed institutions to examine whether they were delivering on constitutional promises around health, housing, water and dignity. Notably, he also suggested that parts of the charter now need revisiting, singling out judicial injunctions he believes frustrate government programmes. At Jeevanjee Gardens, former Chief Justice Willy Mutunga, activist Boniface Mwangi, former Law Society of Kenya president Faith Odhiambo, and others, pushed back hard on that very idea, insisting that talk of amendment serves only those seeking to extend their grip on power, and calling on citizens to defend the docum

title: UN Fact-Finding Mission warns foreign support is fueling Sudan’s war and intensifying civilian suffering
content: The UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Sudan on Thursday released a new report detailing how external support networks fuel the conflict and escalate civilian harm in the country. The Mission concluded that foreign-sourced weapons, drone systems, components, and personnel have significantly expanded the military capabilities of both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), intensifying the conflict’s scale and lethality. According to the report, the RSF and SAF have acquired systems of surveillance and long-distance weapons, including drones , through “externally sourced systems, components, personnel and munitions.” The Mission stressed that international law applies not only to the parties directly engaged in hostilities but also to external actors that violate their obligations under international law when their nationals or entities supply weapons, provide operational support, or facilitate mercenary activity. The Mission notes that drone use has extended the geographical scope of the conflict and is damaging essential infrastructure, including electricity, fuel, water, and transport systems, as well as health systems and public spaces like schools , markets, displacement sites , and places of worship. The report documents RSF drone attacks in El-Obeid , a hospital and school in Kalogoi, and a displacement site in Kulba, impacting civilians “already affected by siege, isolation and restricted access to essential services.” The Mission determined these attacks violated Customary International Humanitarian Law (IHL), which prohibits attacks directed at civilian objects , requires verification that targets are military objectives and requires precautions to minimize civilian harm. SAF drone strikes on a hospital in Ad-Da’ein and strikes on markets in Abu Zaima and Yabus have caused casualties and disrupted commerce and essential services. title: UNICEF reports 20 million children across 21 countries experienced tech-facilitated sexual abuse
content: UNICEF on Thursday reported that nearly one in five internet-using children aged 12 to 17 across 21 countries experienced technology-facilitated sexual exploitation or abuse within a single year, with an estimated 20 million children subjected to at least one form of abuse. The findings expose a substantial enforcement gap fewer than one percent of the experiences were reported to police, social workers or helplines. The agency’s Through Children’s Eyes report found that more than 15 million children encountered unwanted sexual content, nine million were pressured into sexual conversations or sharing sexual images, and four million had sexual images distributed without their consent. Nearly 60 percent of incidents occurred through major social media platforms , while 14 percent involved online games. Notably, 57 percent involved someone the child already knew rather than an unknown online offender. More than four in ten affected children did not share their trauma with anyone else, choosing instead to suffer in silence. Earlier findings from the Disrupting Harm project had already documented similar risks to children online. Its first round surveyed children primarily during 2020-2021 across 12 countries in Africa and Southeast Asia. UNICEF’s new analysis combines those findings with a second round conducted during 2024-2025 in nine additional countries, creating a 21-country dataset covering approximately 21,000 internet-using children. The U.S. National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) recorded 44,155 reports of online enticement , a category that includes sextortion in 2021. That figure rose to 80,524 in 2022 and 186,819 in 2023. NCMEC later reported that in 2024 it received nearly 100 reports of financial sextortion per day on average. Recent prosecutions have also shown how technology-facilitated sexual abuse can involve multiple platforms and victims across different countries. title: Supreme Court asked to review USPS mail ballot rule ahead of midterm elections
content: The Trump Administration on Thursday asked the US Supreme Court to remove a federal judge’s order barring the US Postal Service (USPS) from enforcing new requirements on how states send ballots to voters. The rule in question, enacted by USPS last month under Executive Order 14399 , requires state and local election officials to submit mail ballot envelope designs to USPS for review and to include barcodes and to upload names and addresses of mail voters to a federal portal. Mail ballots that fail to meet these requirements would be rejected under the rule. A federal judge for the US District Court of Massachusetts blocked the enforcement of these requirements via a 14-day temporary restraining order (TRO), making compliance with the rule effectively voluntary. The Supreme Court stayed an earlier injunction in this litigation last week , holding in an unsigned opinion that the states had sued before the administration’s policies were concrete and ripe for review. USPS published the final rule two days later, reopening the matter for judicial review. Thursday’s application faces a jurisdictional hurdle before it can be considered on the merits because TROs are generally not appealable under 28 USC 1292(a)(1) . The application argues that this TRO functions as an appealable injunction because ballots will enter the mail before an ordinary review can run its course. On the merits, the administration argues that the rule “imposes only modest envelope-design and addressee-information requirements,” pointing to USPS authority under 39 USC 401(2) and 404(a)(1) . Opponents argue that the Elections Clause assigns authority over congressional elections to state legislatures and congress itself, hence these requirements exceed USPS authority. The post Supreme Court asked to review USPS mail ballot rule ahead of midterm elections appeared first on JURIST - News .
